prompt: What is reverse ETL?

choices.text: Loading the warehouse from the shop's systems
choices.why: That is the usual direction, ETL.

choices.text: Writing computed numbers back into operational tools
choices.why: Right. Onto the customer's record, where the person doing the work sees it.

choices.text: Undoing a load that went wrong
choices.why: Not what the name means.

choices.text: Exporting a dashboard as a spreadsheet for the board meeting every month
choices.why: That is a report, by hand.

prompt: Why does the salesperson not simply open the dashboard?

choices.text: Dashboards are slower than CRMs
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: Salespeople are not allowed to see revenue
choices.why: Nothing says so.

choices.text: They need one customer's number at the moment they deal with that customer
choices.why: Right. And they spend the day in the CRM.

choices.text: Because the dashboard shows totals for the whole shop rather than one customer
choices.why: A dashboard could show a customer; it is the wrong place.

prompt: According to the lesson, when does a number belong in an operational tool? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Somebody acts on one customer at a time
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The action depends on the number
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The tool does not have the data to compute it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The number is available in the warehouse
choices.why: Available is not a reason; that is how forty fields get sent.

prompt: A customer's region is wrong in the CRM. A salesperson corrects it there by hand. What happens?

choices.text: The correction flows back to the shop's database
choices.why: Nothing flows back from the CRM.

choices.text: The next sync overwrites it
choices.why: Right. The fix belongs in the source; the CRM holds a copy.

choices.text: The sync stops, because the value changed
choices.why: It does not detect edits in the CRM.

choices.text: Nothing; the CRM's value wins forever
choices.why: Only until the next run that sends the field.

prompt: A sync runs every hour. What does the lesson say about "this customer just paid"?

choices.text: Run the sync every minute
choices.why: Not the lesson's answer.

choices.text: Add it to the model
choices.why: It would still be up to an hour late.

choices.text: Send it from the system where it happened
choices.why: Right. Reverse ETL is not real time.

choices.text: Ask the customer to wait an hour
choices.why: No.

prompt: In reverse ETL, what is the model?

choices.text: The query whose rows the destination should hold
choices.why: Right. For Lantern, one row per customer.

choices.text: A machine-learning model that predicts health
choices.why: Here health is a definition in SQL.

choices.text: The CRM's database schema
choices.why: The model is on the warehouse side.

choices.text: The log of what was sent
choices.why: That is `sync_log`.

prompt: Why is health measured from the last day in the data rather than from today's date?

choices.text: Today's date cannot be used in a view
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: It makes every customer look active
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: Because the CRM requires a fixed date for every contact it stores
choices.why: The CRM knows nothing of it.

choices.text: If the data stops, today's date would lapse everybody
choices.why: Right. Lesson 6's rule: the data says when it ends.

prompt: How many of Lantern's customers does the model mark *lapsed*?
Where does the 45-day threshold for *active* come from?

choices.text: Where three gaps in four between orders end
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2 measured the gaps.

choices.text: The CRM's default
choices.why: The CRM has no such default.

choices.text: A month and a half, rounded
choices.why: It was measured, not rounded.

choices.text: The LGPD's retention period for customer data held in a CRM
choices.why: Unrelated.

prompt: Why does the lesson use a pretend CRM?

choices.text: Real CRMs do not have APIs that a script is allowed to call
choices.why: They do; they need accounts and contracts.

choices.text: To build the job with no account or contract
choices.why: Right. It behaves like the APIs a sync has to cope with.

choices.text: Because it is faster than any real one
choices.why: It is deliberately slow.

choices.text: Because real CRMs only accept CSV uploads from a browser, never requests from a script
choices.why: Not true.

prompt: Match each request to what the pretend CRM does with it.

pairs.right: update that key, or create it

pairs.left: more than ten requests in a second

prompt: You stop `crm.py` and start it again. What does it hold, and what must the sync do?

choices.text: Everything, saved to disk; nothing
choices.why: It keeps everything in memory.

choices.text: Half the contacts; resend the other half
choices.why: It holds none.

choices.text: Nothing; `last_sent` is now wrong, so start the memory again
choices.why: Right. The sync's memory says sent, the CRM says empty: running `activation.sql` again starts both from nothing.

choices.text: Nothing; the sync notices the empty CRM on its next run and resends everything
choices.why: It compares with its own memory, not with the CRM.

prompt: Why does the first sync send all 2,649 contacts?

choices.text: `last_sent` is empty
choices.why: Right. Every contact differs from nothing.

choices.text: The script always sends everything
choices.why: The second run sent nothing.

choices.text: The CRM asked for a full copy
choices.why: The CRM asks for nothing.

choices.text: Because the model changed between running activation.sql and running sync.sh
choices.why: It did not.

prompt: Why does the script write to `last_sent` only after the CRM accepts a contact?

choices.text: To save space
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: Because psql cannot write to the database before curl has finished running
choices.why: It could.

choices.text: So a refused contact is tried again next run
choices.why: Right. Remembering before success would mark it sent forever.

choices.text: Because the CRM requires it before it accepts another contact
choices.why: The CRM knows nothing of `last_sent`.

prompt: Why does the script pass values to psql as variables like `:'id'` instead of pasting them into the SQL?

choices.text: psql quotes them safely
choices.why: Right. A value with a quote in it cannot break the statement.

choices.text: It is faster
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: psql cannot read text from a shell variable directly, even inside a heredoc
choices.why: It is about quoting.

choices.text: To keep the password secret
choices.why: No password is involved.

prompt: Why does the diff use `IS DISTINCT FROM` rather than `<>`?

choices.text: `<>` cannot compare JSON
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: `IS DISTINCT FROM` uses the index on `last_sent`, while `<>` reads the whole table each time
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: `<>` with NULL is not true
choices.why: Right. A never-sent contact has a NULL payload, so new contacts would never be sent.

choices.text: It ignores the order of the JSON keys
choices.why: `jsonb` already does that.

prompt: What does a sync that resends every contact every hour cost, besides time?

choices.text: Nothing else
choices.why: It overwrites people's edits every hour.

choices.text: Disk space in PostgreSQL
choices.why: Not the main cost.

choices.text: A second copy of the warehouse
choices.why: No.

choices.text: Requests the API limits, and overwritten edits
choices.why: Right.

prompt: After the new order for customer 1500, how many contacts did the next sync send?
Put reverse ETL's core loop in order.
trap: Remembering before sending is the usual slip: a refused row would count as sent.

prompt: Two POSTs of the same contact left the CRM with three records for `lantern-10`. Who made a mistake?

choices.text: The CRM, which should have refused the second
choices.why: POST means create, so it created.

choices.text: Whoever used POST for a sync
choices.why: Right. A sync upserts by a key; POST creates every time.

choices.text: The network, which duplicated the request
choices.why: Both requests were sent on purpose.

choices.text: Nobody; three records are harmless
choices.why: Each is edited and counted separately.

prompt: Match each candidate key to its problem.

pairs.right: unknown until the CRM creates the record

prompt: Update the record if it exists, create it if not: that operation is called an ___.
A customer is erased from the shop under the LGPD and stays in the CRM. What does the lesson call that?

choices.text: A normal delay
choices.why: The copy is their personal data.

choices.text: An erasure that did not happen
choices.why: Right. The copy in the CRM is personal data as much as the source.

choices.text: A backup
choices.why: It is not kept for recovery.

choices.text: A legitimate archive
choices.why: Nothing makes it legitimate here.

prompt: How does the sync know that customer 2 must be deleted from the CRM?

choices.text: The CRM reports that the customer was erased
choices.why: The CRM knows nothing of the shop.

choices.text: The shop sends a message to the sync
choices.why: Nothing is sent.

choices.text: It deletes every contact and recreates the rest
choices.why: It deletes one.

choices.text: It is in `last_sent` and not in the model
choices.why: Right. The second loop compares the two.

prompt: A contact leaves the model because a filter changed, not because of an erasure. What is the safe default?

choices.text: Delete it, as for an erasure
choices.why: That destroys the notes salespeople wrote.

choices.text: Clear the synced fields and keep the record
choices.why: Right. Delete only when the customer must not be there at all.

choices.text: Leave everything as it was, including the old health
choices.why: Then the CRM shows a value the model no longer stands behind.

choices.text: Stop the sync until someone decides
choices.why: Not the default the lesson gives.

prompt: What does `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 1` ask the sync to do?

choices.text: Give up on the contact
choices.why: It is "not yet", not "never".

choices.text: Wait a second and try again
choices.why: Right. The script does exactly that, up to five times.

choices.text: Retry immediately, as fast as possible
choices.why: That makes the refusal last longer.

choices.text: Change the payload and send it again at once
choices.why: The payload is fine.

prompt: Why should a sync not retry a `400`?

choices.text: Because 400s are rare
choices.why: Frequency is not the point.

choices.text: The CRM bans clients that retry
choices.why: Not in this lesson.

choices.text: The request itself is wrong and fails the same way every time
choices.why: Right. Retry what can succeed later: 429 and server errors.

choices.text: Because it means the network is down, and a retry would only wait for it
choices.why: That would not give a status code.

prompt: What makes the first sync take minutes, and what do commercial tools do instead?

choices.text: One request per contact; they use bulk endpoints
choices.why: Right. A hundred or a thousand records in one request.

choices.text: PostgreSQL is slow; they use another database
choices.why: Not the cause.

choices.text: The model is complex; they skip the model and copy raw tables into the CRM
choices.why: They keep the model.

choices.text: curl is slow; they use a browser
choices.why: No.

prompt: Why is a sync's failure invisible from the CRM?

choices.text: The CRM hides errors
choices.why: It returned them, to the sync.

choices.text: Most rows arrive, and the CRM shows the last successful values
choices.why: Right. Only the sync knows what was refused.

choices.text: Failures delete the contacts
choices.why: They do not.

choices.text: Because the sync runs at night
choices.why: Timing is not the reason.

prompt: After marketing's change, the contacts that became *new* were refused with `400`. What fixes them without resending anything by hand?

choices.text: Deleting them from `last_sent`
choices.why: They were never added to it.

choices.text: Retrying them five times
choices.why: A 400 fails the same way every time.

choices.text: Adding *new* to the CRM's picklist
choices.why: Right. They stayed out of `last_sent`, so the next run sends them.

choices.text: Restarting the CRM
choices.why: That empties it.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a sync without a log is a sync nobody can debug?

choices.text: Logs make the sync faster
choices.why: They do not.

choices.text: The LGPD requires a log of every request a company sends to a vendor
choices.why: Not the lesson's argument.

choices.text: Because the CRM deletes its own history of requests every night at midnight
choices.why: Not stated.

choices.text: When a wrong field is noticed, the request that wrote it is gone
choices.why: Right. The log keeps what happened, run by run.

prompt: Under the LGPD, which principle says send the fields the purpose needs and nothing because it is available?

choices.text: Transparency
choices.why: A real principle, but not this one.

choices.text: Minimisation
choices.why: Right. In the law's own words, necessity.

choices.text: Portability
choices.why: That is a right of the person.

choices.text: Consent
choices.why: A legal basis, not this principle.

prompt: A salesperson edits `health` by hand and sees it undone the next hour. What does the lesson prescribe?

choices.text: Sync less often
choices.why: That delays the problem.

choices.text: Let both write it
choices.why: A field both write is one nobody can rely on.

choices.text: One owner per field: the sync, or people
choices.why: Right. If the sync owns it, the CRM makes it read-only for people.

choices.text: Delete the field
choices.why: It is useful.

prompt: A colleague's sync matches CRM records by e-mail. A customer changes address. What happens at the next run?

choices.text: The record is updated with the new address
choices.why: The new address matches no record.

choices.text: A second record is created for the same customer
choices.why: Right. The key changed, so the upsert found nothing and created.

choices.text: The sync fails with 400
choices.why: The request is valid.

choices.text: Nothing changes
choices.why: Something does: a duplicate.

prompt: Which properties of `sync.sh` does the lesson rely on? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It sends only rows that differ from what was last accepted
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It upserts by the shop's own id
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It retries 429 and logs every attempt
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It reads the CRM before sending, to see what changed there
choices.why: It compares with its own memory, `last_sent`.
